source_text: τὰ δ’ ἑξῆς προςαποδοτέον καὶ τὴν ἐκ τῆς βαρβάρου φιλοσοφίας Ελληνικὴν κλοπὴν σαφέστερον ἤδη παραστατέον. Φασὶ γὰρ σῶμα εἶναι τὸν θεὸν οἱ Στωϊκοὶ καὶ πνεῦμα κατ’ οὐσίαν, ὥσπερ ἀμέλει καὶ τὴν ψυχήν. πάντα ταῦτα ἄντικρυς εὑρήσεις ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς. μὴ γάρ μοι τὰς ἀλληγορίας αὐτῶν ἐννοήσῃς τὰ νῦν ὡς ἡ γνωστικὴ παραδίδωσιν ἀλήθεια, εἰ ἄλλο τι δεικνύουσαι, καθάπερ οἱ σοφοὶ παλαισταί, ἄλλο μηνύουσιν. ἀλλ’ οἳ μὲν διήκειν διὰ πάσης τῆς οὐσίας τὸν θεόν φασιν, ἡμεῖς δὲ ποιητὴν μόνον αὐτὸν καλοῦμεν καὶ λόγῳ ποιητήν. παρήγαγεν δὲ αὐτοὺς τὸ ἐν τῇ Σοφίᾳ εἰρημένον διήκει δὲ καὶ χωρεῖ διὰ πάντων διὰ τὴν καθαριότητα, ἐπεὶ μὴ συνῆκαν λέγεσθαι ταῦτα ἐπὶ τῆς σοφίας τῆς πρωτοκτίστου τῷ θεῷ. ναί, φασίν, ἀλλὰ ὕλην ὑποτίθενται οἱ φιλόσοφοι ἐν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς, οἵ τε Στωϊκοὶ καὶ Πλάτων καὶ Πυθαγόρας, ἀλλὰ καὶ Ἀριστοτέλης ὁ Περιπατητικός, οὐχὶ δὲ μίαν ἀρχήν. ἴστωσαν οὖν τὴν καλουμένην ὕλην ἄποιον καὶ ἀσχημάτιστον λεγομένην πρὸς αὐτῶν, καὶ τολμηρότερον ἤδη μὴ ὂν πρὸς τοῦ Πλάτωνος εἰρῆσθαι. καὶ μή τι μυστικώτατα μίαν τὴν ὄντως οὖσαν ἀρχὴν εἰδὼς ἐν τῷ Τιμαίῳ αὐταῖς φησι λέξεσιν· νῦν δ’ οὖν τὸ παρ’ ἡμῶν ὧδε ἐχέτω· τὴν μὲν περὶ πάντων εἴτε ἀρχὴν εἴτε ἀρχὰς εἴτε ὅπῃ δοκεῖ τούτων πέρι, τὸ νῦν οὐ ῥητέον, δἰ ἄλλο μὲν οὐδέν, διὰ δὲ τὸ χαλεπὸν εἶναι κατὰ τὸν παρόντα τρόπον τῆς διεξόδου δηλῶσαι τὰ δοκοῦντα. ἄλλως τε ἡ λέξις ἡ προφητικὴ ἐκείνη ἡ δὲ γῆ ἦν ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστος ἀφορμὰς αὐτοῖς ὑλικῆς οὐσίας παρέσχηται. Ναὶ μὴν Ἐπικούρῳ μὲν ἡ τοῦ αὐτομάτου παρείσδυσις οὐ παρακολουθήσαντι τῷ ῥητῷ γέγονεν ἐντεῦθεν ματαιότης ματαιοτήτων, τὰ πάντα ματαιότης. Ἀριστοτέλει δὲ μέχρι σελήνης ἐπῆλθε καταγαγεῖν τὴν πρόνοιαν ἐκ τοῦδε τοῦ ψαλμοῦ· κύριε, ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ τὸ ἔλεός σου καὶ ἡ ἀλήθειά σου ἕως τῶν νεφελῶν. οὐδέπω γὰρ ἀποκεκάλυπτο ἡ τῶν προφητικῶν δήλωσις μυστηρίων πρὸ τῆς τοῦ κυρίου παρουσίας. Τάς τε αὖ μετὰ θάνατον κολάσεις καὶ τὴν διὰ πυρὸς τιμωρίαν ἀπὸ τῆς βαρβάρου φιλοσοφίας ἥ τε ποιητικὴ πᾶσα μοῦσα, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ Ἑλληνικὴ φιλοσοφία ὑφείλετο. Πλάτων γοῦν ἐν τῷ τελευταίῳ τῆς Πολιτείας αὐταῖς φησι ταῖς λέξεσιν· ἐνταῦθα δὴ ἄνδρες ἄγριοι, διάπυροι ἰδεῖν, παρεστῶτες, καταμανθάνοντες τὸ φθέγμα, τοὺς μὲν ἰδίᾳ παραλαβόντες ἦγον, τὸν δὲ Ἀριδαῖον καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους συμποδίσαντες χεῖράς τε καὶ πόδας καὶ κεφαλήν, καταβαλόντες καὶ ἐκδείραντες, εἷλκον παρὰ τὴν ὁδὸν ἐκτὸς ἐπ’ ἀσπαλάθων κνάπτοντες. οἱ μὲν γὰρ ἄνδρες οἱ διάπυροι ἀγγέλους αὐτῷ βούλονται δηλοῦν, οἳ παραλαβόντες τοὺς ἀδίκους κολάζουσιν· ὁ ποιῶν, φησί, τοὺς ἀγγέλους αὐτοῦ πνεύματα καὶ τοὺς λειτουργοὺς αὐτοῦ πῦρ φλέγον. ἕπεται δὲ τούτοις τὴν ψυχὴν εἶναι ἀθάνατον. τὸ γὰρ κολαζόμενον ἢ παιδευόμενον ἐν αἰσθήσει ὂν ζῇ, κἂν πάσχειν λέγηται. τί δ’; οὐκ οἶδεν ὁ Πλάτων καὶ πυρὸς ποταμοὺς καὶ τῆς γῆς τὸ βάθος, τὴν πρὸς τῶν βαρβάρων Γέενναν καλουμένην Τάρταρον ποιητικῶς ὀνομάζων, Κωκυτόν τε καὶ Ἀχέροντα καὶ Πυριφλεγέθοντα καὶ τοιαῦτά τινα εἰς τὴν παίδευσιν σωφρονίζοντα παρεισάγων κολαστήρια; τῶν μικρῶν δὲ κατὰ τὴν γραφὴν καὶ ἐλαχίστων τοὺς ἀγγέλους τοὺς ὁρῶντας τὸν θεόν, πρὸς δὲ καὶ τὴν εἰς ἡμᾶς δἰ ἀγγέλων τῶν ἐφεστώτων ἥκουσαν ἐπισκοπὴν ἐμφαίνων οὐκ ὀκνεῖ γράφειν· ἐπειδὴ πάσας τὰς ψυχὰς τοὺς βίους ᾑρῆσθαι, ὥσπερ ἔλαχον, ἐν τάξει προσιέναι πρὸς τὴν Αάχεσιν, κείνην δὲ ἑκάστῳ, ὃν εἵλετο δαίμονα, τοῦτον φύλακα συμπέμπειν τοῦ βίου καὶ ἀποπληρωτὴν τῶν αἱρεθέντων.
pass_a_gloss: The things that follow must be addressed and the Greek theft from barbarian philosophy is to be shown more clearly. For the Stoics say that God is a body and a spirit in essence, just as also the soul. You will find all these things clearly in the scriptures. Do not think of their allegories now as the gnosis delivers truth, if they show something else, just as the ancient wrestlers show something else. But they say that God passes through and penetrates all things, we however call him only the creator and the creator by word. The statement in Wisdom that 'he passes through and penetrates all things because of his purity' led them astray, since they did not understand that these things are said about the primal wisdom of God. Yes, they say, but the philosophers hypothesize matter in the principles, both the Stoics and Plato and Pythagoras, and also Aristotle the Peripatetic, not however one principle. Let them know therefore the so-called matter, uncreated and unformed, as it is said in opposition to them, and more boldly not to be said in opposition to Plato. And does he not say in the Timaeus, knowing the one truly existing principle, in these very words? Now therefore let our discussion be as follows: the matter concerning all things, whether principle or principles or however it seems, is not to be spoken of now, because of nothing else, but because it is difficult to explain the things that seem in the present manner. Besides, the prophetic speech, 'the earth was invisible and unformed', provided them with a basis for material substance. For Epicurus, the idea of spontaneity did not follow from what was said, hence vanity of vanities, all is vanity. And Aristotle drew down providence to the moon from this psalm, 'Lord, your mercy and truth reach to the clouds'. For the explanation of prophetic mysteries had not yet been revealed before the coming of the Lord. The punishments after death and the punishment by fire, and all poetic muse, but also Greek philosophy, borrowed from barbarian philosophy. For Plato, in the last book of the Republic, says in these very words: 'Here indeed wild men, fiery to see, standing, learning the voice, having taken some privately, led them away, but having bound the hands and feet and head of Aridaeus and the others, having thrown them down and flayed them, dragged them along the road outside, striking them with asphalathus'. For the men, the fiery ones, want to indicate angels, who take away the unjust and punish them; he who makes his angels spirits and his servants a burning fire. It follows that the soul is immortal. For what is punished or educated, being in sensation, lives, even if it is said to suffer. What? Does Plato not know of rivers of fire and the depth of the earth, poetically naming the Tartarus of the barbarians, and introducing punishments, such as Cocytus and Acheron and Pyriphlegethon, and such things, for the purpose of education? And concerning the small and least things, according to scripture, the angels who see God, and also the oversight that came to us through the attending angels, he does not hesitate to write: since all souls have chosen their lives, as it were by lot, they come in order to Lachesis, and she sends to each one the demon they chose as a guardian of their life and a fulfiller of their choices.

pass_b_english: We must address what follows and demonstrate more clearly the Greek theft from barbarian philosophy. For the Stoics say that God is a body and a spirit in essence, just as they also say the soul is. You will find all these things plainly in the scriptures. Do not imagine that their allegories now convey truth as the gnosis teaches it, if they show one thing while signaling another, just as ancient wrestlers do. But while they say that God passes through and penetrates all things, we call him only the Creator, and the Creator by his Word. The statement in Wisdom — 'he passes through and penetrates all things because of his purity' (Wisdom 7:27) — led them astray, since they did not understand that these words are spoken of the primal wisdom created by God. Yes, they say, but the philosophers posit matter among their first principles — the Stoics, Plato, Pythagoras, and Aristotle the Peripatetic as well — not a single principle. Let them acknowledge, then, the so-called matter, called uncreated and unformed by them, and even more boldly said not to exist by Plato. And does he not say in the Timaeus, knowing the one truly existing principle, in these very words? Now, therefore, let our discussion stand thus: the question concerning all things, whether principle or principles or whatever one thinks of them, is not to be spoken of now, for no other reason than because it is difficult to explain the things that seem plausible in the present manner. Besides, the prophetic word, 'the earth was invisible and unformed' (Genesis 1:2), provided them with a starting point for material substance.

For Epicurus, the intrusion of chance did not follow from what was said; hence, 'vanity of vanities, all is vanity.' And Aristotle dragged providence down to the moon from this psalm: 'Lord, your mercy is in heaven, and your truth reaches to the clouds' (Psalm 36:5). For the revelation of prophetic mysteries had not yet been disclosed before the coming of the Lord. The punishments after death and the punishment by fire were owed to barbarian philosophy by the whole poetic muse, and by Greek philosophy as well. For Plato, in the last book of the Republic, says in these very words: 'Here indeed wild men, fiery to behold, standing by, perceiving the cry, taking some privately, led them away; but binding the hands and feet and head of Aridaeus and the others, throwing them down and flaying them, they dragged them along the road outside, beating them with thorn-bushes.' The fiery men, he means, represent angels who seize the unjust and punish them — 'who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire.' It follows that the soul is immortal. For what is punished or educated, being in sensation, lives, even if it is said to suffer. What? Does Plato not know of rivers of fire and the depths of the earth, poetically naming the Tartarus of the barbarians, and introducing as correctional punishments for education Cocytus, Acheron, Pyriphlegethon, and such things? And concerning the small and least things according to scripture — the angels who see God, and also the oversight that comes to us through the attending angels — he does not hesitate to write: since all souls have chosen their lives, as it were by lot, they come in order to Lachesis, and she sends to each the demon they chose as a guardian of their life and a fulfiller of their choices.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a polished version with necessary scripture citations (Wisdom 7:27, Genesis 1:2, Psalm 36:5) that match the quoted/alluded content. The translation of 'ἀσπαλάθων' as 'thorn-bushes' in Pass B is a valid interpretation of the material/scrubby ground mentioned in the context of the Republic's description. The identification of 'Αάχεσιν' as 'Lachesis' is contextually correct and noted in the lemmas.

Stromata 14, 'Greek Theft from Barbarian Philosophy', Pass A: 'The things that follow must be addressed and the Greek theft from barbarian philosophy is to be shown more clearly.' Pass B: 'We must address what follows and demonstrate more clearly the Greek theft from barbarian philosophy.'
